question: What is the primary visual output produced by a Computed Tomography scan?

options.A: Real-time dynamic moving videos of the beating heart
options.B: Detailed cross-sectional slice images of internal structures
options.C: Functional metabolic activity maps using radioisotopes
options.D: Flat two-dimensional silhouette shadows of bones

explanation: CT scans use computer processing of multiple X-ray measurements taken from different angles to produce cross-sectional slices of the body. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h1)

question: How does computed tomography fundamentally differ from a standard conventional X-ray?

options.A: Conventional X-rays utilize magnetic fields instead of ionizing radiation
options.B: Computed tomography eliminates the overlapping of structures by producing slice views
options.C: Computed tomography requires no external energy source to generate images
options.D: Standard X-rays provide real-time color functional mapping of soft tissues

explanation: Standard X-rays superimpose all body structures in the path of the beam into a single flat shadow, whereas CT creates distinct slices to separate overlapping organs. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which term describes a structure that absorbs a high amount of radiation and appears bright white on a CT scan?
explanation: Dense tissues such as bone absorb more radiation, allowing fewer X-rays to reach the detectors, which translates to a bright white appearance called hyperdense. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the precise function of the detectors located opposite the rotating X-ray tube in a CT scanner?

options.A: They cool down the gantry system during continuous scanning cycles
options.B: They generate the initial electrical current to power the gantry motor
options.C: They measure the residual radiation intensity after it passes through the patient
options.D: They emit secondary magnetic impulses to stabilize tissue atoms

explanation: The detectors capture the remaining X-ray photons that successfully traverse the body tissues, providing the raw data the computer uses for mathematical reconstruction. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary chemical base used for intravenous contrast media in CT scans?
explanation: Iodine-based contrast agents are safely administered intravenously because they possess high atomic numbers that effectively block X-rays to highlight blood vessels and organs. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why would a clinician order a non-contrast CT scan first for a patient presenting with acute head trauma?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing common allergic skin rashes
options.B: To quickly identify acute blood or bone fractures without waiting for contrast preparation
options.C: Because contrast agents make skull bones completely invisible on scans
options.D: Because intravenous iodine destroys cerebral neurons during active trauma

explanation: Acute hemorrhage naturally appears hyperdense on a baseline non-contrast scan, making urgent identification fast and efficient without delay or added contrast risks. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h3)

question: Why is an urgent non-contrast CT scan mandatory for a patient presenting with acute stroke symptoms before medical treatment begins?

options.A: To rule out an active intracranial hemorrhage before giving clot-busting medications
options.B: To diagnose underlying bacterial meningitis causing the neurological deficit
options.C: To calculate the total circulating blood volume in the brain
options.D: To measure the exact intracranial pressure within the ventricles

explanation: Giving thrombolytic therapy to a patient experiencing a hemorrhagic stroke can be fatal; the CT scan confirms whether the stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h4)

question: A motor vehicle accident victim arrives at the emergency ward with unstable vital signs and rigid abdominal guarding. Which diagnostic procedure is most urgently indicated?

options.B: Routine chest radiography in the upright position
options.C: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis
options.D: Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine

explanation: A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard for rapidly visualizing solid organ injuries and active internal bleeding in trauma patients. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h4)

question: Which laboratory parameter is most critical for a nurse to review prior to administering intravenous contrast for a CT scan?
explanation: Serum creatinine reflects renal function; impaired kidneys struggle to excrete iodine-based contrast, increasing the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h5)

question: A patient scheduled for a contrast-enhanced CT scan has a prescription for metformin to manage type 2 diabetes. What is the appropriate nursing action regarding this medication?

options.A: Discontinue metformin permanently because it is permanently contraindicated
options.B: Withhold metformin on the day of the scan and coordinate instructions regarding post-procedure resumption
options.C: Administer the medication intravenously right before the scan begins
options.D: Double the morning dose to compensate for hospital fasting

explanation: Metformin is typically held around the time of iodinated contrast administration to avoid the rare risk of lactic acidosis if temporary kidney injury occurs. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary reason patients are instructed to remain completely motionless during a CT scan?

options.A: To avoid motion artifact which blurs and ruins the diagnostic quality of the images
options.B: To prevent the motorized table from locking up due to shifting weight
options.C: To keep the patient's heart rate stable throughout the imaging sequence
options.D: To prevent accidental dislodgement of the intravenous line

explanation: Even slight movements by the patient can cause blurring, known as motion artifact, making fine details and small lesions difficult for the radiologist to interpret. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h6)

question: What immediate nursing action is required if a patient begins complaining of a severe metallic taste, generalized flushing, and mild nausea right as intravenous contrast starts flowing?

options.A: Immediately stop the CT scanner and call a code blue emergency
options.B: Clamp the intravenous line and flush with sterile water
options.C: Reassure the patient that a warm flush and metallic taste are common, expected side effects

explanation: A transient flush of warmth and a metallic taste are normal physiological sensations associated with the rapid injection of iodinated contrast media and do not indicate anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary nursing intervention recommended immediately after a patient undergoes a contrast-enhanced CT scan?

options.A: Perform a neurological assessment every fifteen minutes
options.B: Encourage high fluid intake to facilitate renal excretion of the contrast
options.C: Keep the patient strictly fasting for an additional six hours
options.D: Apply a cold compress to the intravenous insertion site

explanation: Increasing fluid intake helps flush the nephrotoxic iodinated contrast media rapidly out of the kidneys, reducing the risk of renal injury. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h7)

question: A patient who received oral barium sulfate for a abdominal CT scan calls the ward concerned because their stool is pale and whitish. What is the correct nursing response?

options.A: Withhold all future oral fluids until normal brown stool color returns
options.B: Reassure the patient that this is a normal temporary elimination pattern after barium ingestion
options.C: Report this finding immediately as an indicator of severe internal gastrointestinal bleeding
options.D: Advise the patient to report to the emergency department for immediate gastric lavage

explanation: Barium sulfate is a white metallic compound that passes through the gastrointestinal tract largely unchanged, giving stools a pale or whitish appearance until fully cleared. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h7)

question: What acronym guides healthcare professionals in minimizing patient radiation exposure during diagnostic imaging procedures?
explanation: The ALARA principle stands for 'As Low As Reasonably Achievable', directing staff to use the lowest possible radiation dose required to obtain diagnostic-quality images. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h8)

question: Why are ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging generally preferred over CT scans when diagnosing conditions in pregnant women?

options.A: CT scanners cannot accommodate the physical weight of pregnant patients
options.B: Intravenous contrast agents are completely harmless to the developing fetus
options.C: Pregnant women are universally allergic to all forms of radiographic equipment
options.D: Ultrasound and MRI completely avoid the use of ionizing radiation

explanation: To protect the developing fetus from potential risks associated with ionizing radiation, non-ionizing modalities like ultrasound and MRI are selected when clinically feasible. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T13#GNS123_U2_T13_h8)
